title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
tagline: From O(n²) DP to an elegant O(n log n) patience-sorting trick.

intuition.analogy: Playing solitaire 'patience': deal cards onto piles where each new card goes on the leftmost pile whose top is ≥ it (or starts a new pile). The number of piles equals the length of the longest increasing run you could form.
paragraphs: The LIS is the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase. The simple DP defines dp[i] = longest increasing subsequence ending at i, computed by scanning all earlier smaller elements — that's O(n²).

The faster method keeps an array 'tails', where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail value of any increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each value you binary-search the first tail ≥ it: if none, you extend (a longer LIS is possible); otherwise you overwrite that tail with the smaller value, keeping options open for the future.
tails is always sorted, so binary search applies, giving O(n log n). Its length is the LIS length (though tails itself is not necessarily a valid subsequence).
intuition.keyIdea: Keep the smallest tail for each achievable length; binary-search where each new value fits — extend or improve.

steps.title: Maintain tails
steps.detail: tails[k] = minimum tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. Initially empty.

steps.title: Binary search each element
steps.detail: For value x, find the first index in tails with value ≥ x (lower_bound).

steps.title: Extend or replace
steps.detail: If x is larger than all tails, append it (LIS grew). Otherwise overwrite tails[pos] = x to keep tails minimal.

steps.title: Answer
steps.detail: The length of tails is the LIS length.

dryRun.clickMoment: When 3 overwrites 5, the LIS length doesn't change — but the tail becomes smaller, leaving more room for future values like 7 to extend. That 'keep tails minimal' instinct is the whole trick.

approach: Patience sorting: keep `tails`, where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.
For each value, binary-search its insertion point in tails; replace or append. The length of tails is the LIS length.

problems.hint: Sort by width asc, height desc; LIS on heights.

approach: Sort by width ascending, breaking ties by height descending. Then the answer is the LIS over heights — the tie-break stops equal-width envelopes from nesting.
Apply the O(n log n) patience LIS to the height sequence.

problems.title: Number of LIS
problems.statement: Count how many longest increasing subsequences exist.
problems.hint: O(n²) DP tracking both length and count.

approach: Track two arrays: length[i] (LIS ending at i) and count[i] (number of such LIS).
For j < i with a[j] < a[i]: if it extends to a longer subsequence, copy the count; if it ties the best length, add the count. Sum counts of maximal length.

problems.title: Longest String Chain
problems.statement: Longest chain where each word adds one letter.
problems.hint: Sort by length; DP like LIS over predecessor words.

approach: Sort words by length. dp[w] = longest chain ending at w; try removing each character to form a predecessor and extend its best chain.
Hash-map dp keyed by word; answer is the maximum chain length.

problems.title: Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids
problems.statement: Max stack height under dimension constraints.
problems.hint: Sort dimensions, then a LIS-like DP.

approach: Sort each cuboid's dimensions so any face can be the base, then sort cuboids. Now stacking is a 3-D 'all dimensions non-increasing' LIS.
dp[i] = max height with cuboid i on top; for j < i where all dims of j <= dims of i, dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j]) + height_i.
